wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
hazards: the same ford, avalanche-debris zone and brushy climbers' path as the standard approach
a descent onto a large crevassed icefield with the return climb still to come
a long traverse beneath a face, exposed to anything coming off it
a bergschrund at the base of the face
a shaded north aspect that holds hard ice and cold, with a committing position
an approach that reaches its base by losing height, so retreat means re-climbing
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.baseFinding:
The defining instruction is that you do not turn uphill at the col the standard route uses. From the glacier col, descend onto the big icefield and keep traversing east beneath the peak. The base of this route is out on that ice, under the face, not at any saddle.

If you have climbed to a col with a bergschrund on it and are looking at an easy snowfield contouring round to a sunny side, you have arrived at the standard route's entry at about 7,640 ft and gone past your own. Drop back onto the ice and continue east under the wall.

The aspect is the other test and it is unambiguous. This face is the shaded side. If the wall above you is in morning or afternoon sun while the icefield behind you is bright, you are round on the southern flank and looking at the wrong ground. The face should be holding shadow when the rest of the basin is not.

And check the mountain, not just the face. This summit sits just under a mile east of its larger and better-known neighbour along the connecting crest, and the same icefield runs beneath both. A north face reached quickly after crossing the first col is the neighbour's; keep traversing until the summit above you is the eastern one.

Watch the bergschrund at the foot of the face, which is a separate feature from the one on the standard route's col and behaves differently through the season.

wa_sinister_peak_north_face.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
hazards: long committed glacier travel with no camp of its own
crevasses across the whole traverse
exposure beneath a face for the length of the approach
a bergschrund at the foot of the wall
a plan that only makes sense inside a larger traverse, so a retreat is a multi-day proposition
wa_sinister_peak_north_face.baseFinding:
Arriving from the west, the icefield is the highway and the peak is picked off it. Traverse east along the ice beneath the crest until the summit above you is the eastern of the two on this section of ridge - the larger, better-known peak lies just under a mile to the west, so the first big north face you pass is not yours.

The face is the shaded one. If the wall you are approaching takes direct sun while the ice around you is in shadow, you are on the wrong aspect or the wrong peak.

The base is on the ice itself, beneath the wall, with a bergschrund at the junction. There is no col involved - if you have climbed to a saddle to reach your start, you have joined the standard route's entry on the far side of the crest instead.

Because this arrival involves no fixed camp of its own, fix a retreat plan before crossing beneath the face: the ground you traverse in to reach it is the ground you must reverse to leave, and it is all crevassed.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.baseFinding: The route is entered at a col, and there are two cols in a row - getting the order right is the navigation. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the first glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow. Cross over the first col, then descend the second, larger glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right - eastward - across it. The col you want is at about 7,640 ft and it sits between this peak and its larger neighbour to the west. A bergschrund guards it and can be hard to cross late in the season, sometimes needing a short rappel to get down onto or across it. The schrund is the confirmation as much as the obstacle: a col reached without one is likely the first col, not the second. The positive test at the col is where you go next: contour on an easy snowfield round to the peak's south side and climb a loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge. If you are still on the north or shaded side of the crest with the face above you, you have not contoured far enough round. The most important negative marker is about which mountain you are on. The summit lies just under a mile east of its better-known neighbour along the connecting ridge. If you have topped out on the summit block immediately above the first col you crossed, you are on the neighbour, not on this peak. Keep going east. There is also a direct alternative from the col: an exposed class 3+ ridge taken straight from the saddle instead of the gully. Both finish on the same crest; the gully is the standard and the loose rock in it is the main hazard on the climb.

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col
wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route.baseFinding:
Either camp feeds the same line: traverse the upper basins near 7,000 ft to gain the first glacier, cross its col, descend the second glacier to about 7,200 ft, and traverse east to the 7,640 ft col between this peak and its neighbour.

Count the cols. The first is crossed and the second is the destination, with a bergschrund on it. Standing at a col with a large icefield behind you and the summit block immediately above is the first col and the neighbouring peak, not this one.

From the correct col, contour round on easy snow to the peak's south side and find the loose gully. A route that climbs directly out of the col on exposed class 3+ crest is the direct variant rather than the standard, so choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

If you camped at the lake, budget the extra height gain into the morning; if you camped on the ridge, budget the wind into the night.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
hazards: Unmaintained, unsigned ridge path beyond the pass
No water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
Loose, deteriorating black rock on upper pitch 2 and on the ridge approach
Slick granite when wet
Snow persists on the approach trail into July; mosquitoes severe in lake basins in early summer
Two rappels back to the base; loose pointy rocks and exposure on the summit slab
Long round trip commits a day attempt to a late finish
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.baseFinding:
The pass is the gate and the climbers' path leaves directly from the top of it. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs south along the ridge from the pass itself. If you are casting about on the trail below the pass for a junction, you have not got high enough.

The tower is a distinct rock tower on that crest and it is the first one. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the north-east side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

The critical negative marker is the mountain further along the same ridge. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, you have continued to the mountain and gone past the tower. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

The route confirms itself on the second pitch: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one diagonalling left into a gully and finishing at a large boulder near the top. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is two short pitches of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. No campfires above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
hazards: More climbing than the crest-trail option, entirely in forest with little view of weather ahead
Unmaintained, unsigned ridge path beyond the pass
No water on the ridge beyond the pass
Loose, deteriorating black rock on upper pitch 2
Slick granite when wet
Snow persists on the approach into July; mosquitoes in lake basins in early summer
Two rappels back to the base; loose pointy rocks and exposure on the summit slab
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.baseFinding:
From the pass the approach is identical to the other trailhead's: an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the top of the pass and runs south along the ridge.

The tower is the first distinct rock formation on that crest, and its north-east face looks back toward the pass. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

The negative marker is the same and it is the one that matters: the mountain lies further along the same ridge, above a lake basin. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

Confirm on the climb itself: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling left into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)

bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.
bivy.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
bivy.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.
bivy.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is usually reported as the required parking permit, though not universally; carry one.
bivy.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Rough, narrow FR 4096 spur; high clearance helps
Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in a brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your right for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk: deep, cold and fast in early season; log jams move year to year
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier
Rockfall and loose rock on the Corkscrew shelf and summit block, worse with parties stacked in the gully
Low-5th-class exposed step about 100 ft below the summit, downclimbed on the way back
Moat falls on the glacier edge have caused a documented accident
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your right, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.baseFinding:
The camp is found by refusing a summit. The climbers' path leads toward Pyramid Peak and the correct move is to drop slightly before it and traverse across scree and boulders to the moraine. If you have scrambled to a summit, you have climbed the wrong peak and gone past the traverse. The arrival marker is a meltwater tarn sitting against a terminal moraine with the ice above it.

From camp the route is a sequence of three pieces of ground and they must come in order. First, rope up before leaving camp and climb the Colonial Glacier south past a rock feature on its east flank, on snow up to about thirty degrees, working around the moraine lake to a broad col near 6,840 ft. A stream runs at that col - a saddle with no water on it is not the right one.

Second, from the col you drop roughly 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. If you are still gaining height after the col, you have not found the crossing. This is the stretch with no reference points, so track your line for the return; whiteout navigation here is the standing problem of the route.

Third, leave the glacier on the peak's north-west side near a prominent rock feature around 7,700 ft and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. That puts you three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit. If you are still on ice with the summit pyramid rising straight above you and no gully beside it, you have crossed too far and are under the face rather than the ridge.

The finish is a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and blocky scrambling. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge
wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier.baseFinding:
The col is identified by three things at once: it is broad, it has a stream on it, and the ground beyond it drops onto a second, much larger glacier. A saddle that is dry, or one with nothing but rock beyond it, is not this col.

From camp the first move is downhill - 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve - and then a roped crossing on which the cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field. Bridges are usually sound by midsummer and need active route-finding around open slots. Mark your outbound line. Coming back to a col you cannot see, across ground with no features, is the part of this route that goes wrong.

Leave the ice on the peak's north-west side around 7,700 ft, near the prominent rock feature there, and take the class 3 gully with its single exposed rib crossing onto the west ridge, three to four hundred feet below the summit. If there is no gully where you step off the ice, you have gone too far across.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.baseFinding:
The hardest thing to find on this approach is the path itself, and it is found at a firepit. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ends at a small clearing with an old firepit. The climbers' path leaves on the left near that clearing, unsigned and steep from its first step. Fix the spot in your mind on the way in - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

The second decision is a cairned fork near 5,200 ft. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; stay right and uphill on the climbers' path. If you are losing height toward water, you have taken the fisherman's trail.

Expect to lose the tread on the ridge and not to panic about it. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. When in doubt, stay on the crest.

The climb proper starts above the lake meadows. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A rock wall lines the east side of that outlet; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

Rope up before stepping onto the snow, not part-way across. If you are trying to climb a rock wall beside the outlet stream, you have missed the turn around its end.

wa_snowking_mountain_standard.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
wa_snowking_mountain_standard.baseFinding:
Whichever camp you use, the climb starts at the head of the lake's outlet stream. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A rock wall runs along the east side of it - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of that wall with a single class 3 step. Forcing the wall directly is the wrong answer and is how parties get stopped here.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

The arrival test is the notch, not the angle. You should step down into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the left, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.

wa_south_arete.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
wa_south_arete.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes
wa_south_arete.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other. The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.

wa_south_arete.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
wa_south_arete.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter
wa_south_arete.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe easier to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the right, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.baseFinding: The buttress toe is the low point of the prow, sitting immediately left of the gully that separates North from South Early Winters Spire — so you find it by first locating that dividing gully and then stepping left out of it, rather than by heading straight up from the talus. The first pitch is rambling 5.6 with moss, dirt and some loose rock; a scruffy easy pitch is the correct start here, and if your first pitch is clean and steep you are too high on the buttress or on one of the harder east-side lines. The last large tree in the centre of Spire Gully is the checkpoint before this: if you are still climbing the gully and have passed no such tree, you have not reached the traverse point yet.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_.baseFinding: Snow does not move the buttress toe — it is still the low point of the prow just left of the North/South Early Winters dividing gully. What it changes is the traverse: on snow the rightward traverse from the last large tree in the gully is a straightforward but exposed snow crossing rather than a talus scramble, and the transition back onto rock at the base of the buttress will likely involve a moat. Fix the dividing gully visually from the highway before you start — from inside a snowy Spire Gully in flat light the individual features all read the same.

wa_south_face_10.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_south_face_10.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
wa_south_face_10.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Roughly 12-mile trail approach to Andrews Pass, over an old burn that is hot, rocky and buggy with no shade
Several routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat
wa_south_face_10.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

First, rule out the tower. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the open wall, and specifically on its centre. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a spectacular curving chimney — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

Negative marker, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.

Second negative marker: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

wa_south_face_10.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_south_face_10.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_south_face_10.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
Wall foreshortens from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
Loose rock and grainy granite in places
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat
wa_south_face_10.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached tower at the lower right of the wall; the deep gully between that tower and the mountain; and the open centre of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the curving chimney at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

Negative marker from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

wa_south_face_10.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_south_face_10.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Very long approach: Chewuch River trail nearly to Remmel Lake, then a climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin
Loose rock and grainy granite in places; rockfall from parties above
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk; far from rescue
Afternoon thunderstorms; grizzly bear habitat

wa_south_gully_south_spur.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

wa_south_gully_south_spur.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
wa_south_gully_south_spur.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds; helmet from the talus upward
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
Huge cliffs on the approach; the start of the gully lies about 100 ft left of them
Whiteout route-finding on the winter approach
wa_south_gully_south_spur.baseFinding:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

wa_south_gully_south_spur.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
wa_south_gully_south_spur.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
wa_south_gully_south_spur.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall very likely with a documented fatal history
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully; helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant
Private property on the walking approach is closed to climbers; no-parking signs on the road
Chockstone and moat problems; verglas on rock in cold shoulder seasons
wa_south_gully_south_spur.baseFinding:
The gully is the obvious one on the south side, and the test is that it forces you out left. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

The confirmation is the chockstone, and it comes early. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' left out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

What the rock should feel like: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

And the negative test against its neighbours: the big west face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

wa_south_spur.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
wa_south_spur.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season
wa_south_spur.baseFinding:
The route starts where the camp ends: from Perfect Pass, head north and up onto the broad south snowfield. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a conspicuous col in the summit ridge above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

So the aiming point is a notch in a skyline, and in cloud the substitute for it is this: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow runs out against rock. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

Confirm above: the final stretch along the crest is short, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

The variation that is not an error: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the northeast of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

The impasse, which is the other thing you have to find on this approach: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.

wa_south_spur.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
camps: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_south_spur.notes:
An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
wa_south_spur.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
wa_south_spur.baseFinding:
This variant is defined by what it avoids, and that is the test: if you have crossed the impasse, you are not on it. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

Arrival is the same arrival: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

What you trade for it, and why the choice is a conditions call rather than a preference: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.

wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.baseFinding:
The col between the two Mox summits is the whole navigation, and the trap is that there are two summits. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

At the col, check which tower you are under. This route is on the eastern summit, which is the harder and higher of the pair. If the peak above you is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, you are facing the western summit and have turned the wrong way out of the saddle.

The sequence above the col is a ladder of specific shapes, in order, and it is how you know you are right: a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief descent to a small flat area. The flat spot after a downclimb is the confirmation - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

From that flat area, locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. If you are uncoiling a rope at the col itself, you are hundreds of feet too low.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib.baseFinding:
From either camp the route meets at the same place: the saddle between the two Mox summits, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

The high camp's own marker is that it sits on rock outcrops at the glacier's edge at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

At the saddle, the summit you want is the eastern one - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

The confirmation sequence is the same ladder: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short downclimb to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.
